assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include sufficiently granular dimensions, stable segmentation keys, timestamps, or other quasi-identifiers that permit correlation by the partner.

title: Aggregated analytics may still reveal identifiable individuals or small groups
description: Aggregation does not automatically prevent identifiability. If reports are broken down by narrow cohorts, geography, time window, feature usage, or campaign, the partner may infer information about a specific user or a very small group, especially when combined with external knowledge.
assumptions: Assumes some analytics slices may have low counts or high dimensionality, making re-identification or singling out feasible.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; applicability depends on the granularity and minimum group sizes of the shared analytics.

title: Partner can infer sensitive interests or behavior from engagement analytics
description: Usage and engagement analytics sent to the advertising/analytics partner can allow the recipient to infer user interests, habits, or potentially sensitive app-usage patterns. Even when data is aggregated, repeated or segmented reports may disclose information about protected or sensitive categories associated with parts of the user base.
assumptions: Assumes the app domain or feature-level engagement metrics are semantically revealing enough to support inference.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; disclosure risk depends on the semantics of the app and the detail of the analytics shared.

title: Users may be unaware that backend analytics are shared with an advertising partner
description: Sharing analytics with an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier may be insufficiently visible to users, especially if the transfer happens server-side rather than directly from the app. Users may therefore be unable to understand who receives data and for what purpose.
assumptions: Assumes notices are incomplete, unclear, or not presented at the point where users can reasonably understand the sharing.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; this is a strong fit conceptually for unawareness in third-party analytics sharing.

title: Analytics sharing for advertising funding may exceed consent or stated purpose
description: If users did not freely consent to third-party analytics sharing, or if the privacy notice frames analytics as service improvement while the actual purpose includes monetization or advertising support, this flow may violate consent, purpose-limitation, or transparency requirements.
assumptions: Assumes the legal basis, consent mechanism, or privacy notice may not explicitly cover sharing aggregated analytics with an advertising/analytics partner for monetization.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate because the retrieved context does not include detailed non-compliance subnodes; legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and implementation details.

title: Check-in/SOS message enables linkability of the child's events over time
description: The manual check-in / SOS message contains the child's identity context and current location. Repeated submissions can be linked to the same child, allowing correlation of movements, routines, and emergency events across time.
assumptions: The backend can associate incoming messages with a persistent child account, device identifier, or session.

title: SOS message reveals identifying and sensitive location information
description: The child sends a message that directly or indirectly identifies them and includes precise current location. This exposes highly sensitive personal data about whereabouts and potentially distress/emergency status.
assumptions: The payload includes or is associated with a child identifier and sufficiently precise location data.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability node citation was not in the retrieved context; node id is selected by best judgement.

title: SOS submission creates attributable evidence that the child sent the message
description: The backend may store the check-in / SOS request together with account, device, timestamp, and location metadata, creating evidence that can be attributed to the child as sender.
assumptions: The system logs or stores the incoming message with identifiers or metadata tying it to the child/device.

title: Current location and SOS content disclose the child's whereabouts and situation
description: The data flow discloses personal information beyond mere identity: the child's real-time location and the fact that they initiated a manual check-in or SOS. This can reveal home/school patterns, travel, and possible vulnerability or distress.
assumptions: Location is transmitted with enough precision to infer meaningful places or patterns.
uncertainty_note: Specific Detectability/Disclosure tree node citation was not retrieved; node id is based on best judgement for disclosure of personal information.

title: Transmission of a manual check-in/SOS may be detectable by observers
description: An observer of network traffic or system activity may detect that the child has sent a check-in or SOS event, even if message contents are protected. The mere occurrence and timing of such an event can reveal that the child is active, at risk, or following a routine.
assumptions: Traffic metadata, message timing, or endpoint communication patterns are observable to some party.

title: Collection of precise child location for SOS/check-in may exceed necessity or valid consent
description: The backend receives precise real-time location and emergency/check-in status from a child, which is high-risk data. If the system lacks an appropriate legal basis, age-appropriate consent/authorization, purpose limitation, minimization, or retention controls, this flow may be non-compliant with privacy obligations.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires special protections for children's location data and emergency-related data.
